title: Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s Elizabeth Holmes Doc ‘You Can See Everything’ Detonates the Oscar Race — and Has A24 Chasing a 90-Year Record
description: For three days, the Telluride Film Festival ran on a single unknown rumor. By Sunday night, the line outside the Werner Herzog Theatre had swelled i
body:
For three days, the Telluride Film Festival ran on a single unknown rumor. By Sunday night, the line outside the Werner Herzog Theatre had swelled into the longest of the weekend, phones were sealed in locked pouches, a security team worked the aisles in night-vision goggles and a Telluride programmer took the stage to warn the crowd, only half-joking, that anyone who spoiled what came next was no longer loved. Then the mystery that had consumed the mountains finally broke. The secret screening was “You Can See Everything,” Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s documentary about Elizabeth Holmes, and the room came apart.
	

	A24 confirmed it the same night as the movie hit play, dropping a teaser and announcing an October theatrical release, which means the guessing game is over and the awards conversation has begun. With that release date, the studio has planted a 172-minute nonfiction epic squarely in this season’s documentary feature race — and it arrives as the rare title that critics and attendees started debating immediately after the credits finished.


	Thirty-four days before she reported to prison, Holmes invited a skeptical crew inside her home to record her every move. What began as a portrait of a convicted felon became a three-year descent that A24’s own logline calls a journey “into the abyss.” Hollywood has chased the Theranos saga for years — Alex Gibney’s “The Inventor” got there in 2019, Hulu’s “The Dropout” won Amanda Seyfried an Emmy and a Jennifer Lawrence vehicle from Adam McKay collapsed before it could even start shooting — but no one has approached Holmes the way these two filmmakers do.
	

	That is the first reason to take this seriously as a contender. Fielder is the most restlessly inventive nonfiction mind in television, coming off a second season of “The Rehearsal” that earned Peabody recognition and an Emmy nomination for writing and “You Can See Everything” is his feature directing debut. Oppenheim, meanwhile, is having the festival run of his life — his first scripted feature, the Robert Pattinson thriller “Primetime,” bowed in Venice to a rapturous response — and his nonfiction pedigree (“Some Kind of Heaven,” “Ren Faire,” “Spermworld”) gives the project a formal rigor that Fielder’s persona-driven work does not always foreground.

	The pairing is the story. Two artists obsessed with how the camera warps the thing it records, turned loose on the most studied liar of the century.

	The craft is what builds an awards case, and this one is stacked. Shot by David Bolen — the “Some Kind of Heaven” and “Thelma” cinematographer who also lensed Oppenheim’s “Primetime” — the film trades the filmmakers’ usual anamorphic gloss for a boxed-in 4:3 frame and long zoom lenses that let two operators drift through a family home like ghosts, but ones the families clearly acknowledge and want as part of their story. Editor Adam Locke-Norton, Fielder’s collaborator of two decades, sustains conversations well past the point of comfort, letting non-answers hang in the air. And Ari Balouzian, the composer and one-third of the soul trio Gabriels, threads a noir score through the domestic footage that turns a beach house into a crime scene of the mind.

	In a documentary field where craft branches increasingly reward ambition, all three are legitimate below-the-line conversation starters.



	

					You Can See Everything
									Courtesy of A24
	



	Then there is the thing itself, which plays less like a true-crime doc than a controlled experiment in whether a viewer can tell honesty from performance. Fielder does not stay behind the lens for long. Drawn into the frame by his subjects and by his own need to interject, he becomes the film’s destabilized center — a filmmaker visibly struggling, in real time, to work out whether he is being played.

	The result is a movie that keeps escalating in strangeness across its three-year span and lands a final movement that had Telluride’s most seasoned attendees walking out shell-shocked. “Wild” and “WTF?” were the words circulating on the gondola line, and they were compliments.
	

	Which brings us to the hurdles, because they are significant. The documentary branch has never fully made peace with participatory, comedy-adjacent nonfiction and voters who prize the observational and the earnest may recoil from a film in which the director is this present and this implicated.

	There are obviously lingering questions about how much of it is “scripted” — which will spark debates over whether an acting nomination can come from such a movie, because the central performance that surprises in the film is, in fact, eligible for Oscar recognition, Variety has confirmed, although not for SAG.

	A24 insiders see hurdles in the documentary branch, which is why they’re eyeing this film as a — wait for it — Best Picture play. And why the hell not?

	With A24’s arsenal of contenders this year — which could include the summer hit “The Invite,” the Cannes breakout “Club Kid” and the Telluride debut smash “The Debut” — is there a real path for the indie studio to challenge the record for the most Best Picture nominations by a single studio in one year?

	That record belongs to Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer, which landed five at the ninth Academy Awards in 1937. A24 still has Chris Rock’s “Misty Green” to come out of Toronto, and it just dropped the aforementioned “Primetime” at Venice.

	MGM achieved the feat when the Academy was nominating 10 films in the Best Picture category. “The Great Ziegfeld” was the big winner, taking home three statues. It was joined by four other MGM releases from 1936: “Libeled Lady,” “Romeo and Juliet,” “San Francisco” and “A Tale of Two Cities.”

	At the time, MGM was the undisputed heavyweight in Hollywood, home to top talents such as Clark Gable, Judy Garland, Spencer Tracy, Greta Garbo, Joan Crawford, Jean Harlow and Norma Shearer. So expansive was the A-list roster that the studio famously boasted it had “more stars than there are in heaven.”

	But the bigger record is hidden inside all of this.

	A documentary has never been nominated for best picture across 98 ceremonies. When the Academy expanded the field to as many as 10 nominees in 2009, it pointed to exactly this kind of nonfiction (and animated) filmmaking as newly able to compete. Seventeen years later, it still hasn’t happened for documentaries; only three animated films have ever cracked the category.
	

	A Best Picture nomination for “You Can See Everything” wouldn’t merely pad A24’s tally — it would make history as the first documentary ever nominated for the Academy’s top prize.

	The 172-minute runtime is a genuine ask. And there is the subject herself: Platforming a convicted fraudster, even to interrogate her, invites the accusation of handing Holmes a stage and any campaign will have to make the case — loudly — that the film indicts rather than rehabilitates.

	The smartest defense is baked into the movie’s DNA. This is not a redemption tour. It is a study of the impossibility of ever knowing what is real, which is either the perfect subject for a branch that fetishizes authenticity or a provocation aimed straight at it.

	A24 has the muscle to fight that fight. The studio has run documentary campaigns before and knows how to convert festival heat into a shortlist slot, and the fall precursor calendar gives it a runway — the Gotham Awards, the IDA Documentary Awards, Critics Choice Documentary, Cinema Eye Honors and the DGA’s documentary prize all feed the Oscar shortlist and a film this discussed will not want for coverage.

	The October release is early enough to build, and the Fielder factor guarantees a level of press attention most nonfiction contenders would kill for.

	The bottom line is that the documentary race, whatever shape it was taking a week ago, now has to reckon with this. A movie about the impossibility of trust, made with the person least equipped to earn it, dropped without warning into a festival built on the honor system — the metaphors write themselves, and so, most likely, will the ballots of a lot of voters who cannot stop thinking about it.

	“I’m not that person,” Holmes insists in the teaser. “I can promise you that.”

	By the time the lights came up in Telluride, nobody in the room was sure whether to believe her.

schema.headline: Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s Elizabeth Holmes Doc ‘You Can See Everything’ Detonates the Oscar Race — and Has A24 Chasing a 90-Year Record

title: Film Industry Leaders Demand Structural Fix for Gender Gap at Lumiere Summit
description:
Women held 17% of key behind-camera roles when the Celluloid Ceiling study began tracking the figure in 1998. 

	Last year, that number stood at 23%
body:
Women held 17% of key behind-camera roles when the Celluloid Ceiling study began tracking the figure in 1998. 

	Last year, that number stood at 23%. Six points in 27 years. That statistic opened a panel at the Lumière Summit on Monday titled “Safer Sets, Different Stories: Why Gender Balance Matters,” where leaders from StudioCanal, Canal+, the BFI, the Berlinale and the Toronto Film Festival called for structural accountability measures and argued that the failure to include women is as much a creative loss as a moral one.
	

	“The cinema industry should not be considering this as a constraint or a concession,” said Anna Marsh, chief executive of Studiocanal and deputy chief executive of Canal+. “It should be about cinema investing in its own future.” Fifty percent of film school graduates are women, Marsh noted, but by the time filmmakers reach their third feature, only one in six directors is a woman. A woman director’s budget runs, on average, at 44% of that assigned to a male director. Canal+ has extended its development budget by €1 million over three years specifically to finance projects from female writers and directors, Marsh said, and a film about silent cinema pioneer Alice Guy, to be directed by Anne Le Ny, is in development.


	Ben Roberts, director general of the British Film Institute, drew on the BFI’s own Sight and Sound “Greatest Films of All Time” poll to make the case. In 2012, just three of the top 100 films were directed by women; by 2022, that had risen to 11, with two each by Agnès Varda and Chantal Akerman. “That tells me two things,” Roberts said. “Women are as capable, if not more capable, than men of making incredible cinema. So, the inequality is tragic.” He pointed to the BFI’s Inclusion Standards, dating from around 2014, and the new Creative Industries Independent Standards Authority as structural measures. “Work travels, employment travels,” Roberts said, calling on international co-production partners to align on shared minimum standards.
	

	Berlinale festival director Tricia Tuttle cited her own festival’s data. In 2005, women directed 0% of films in Berlinale competition. By 2015 that had reached 15%, and by 2025 it stood at 40%. “Transparency makes you very aware, as a curator and as a decision-maker and a cultural gatekeeper, of what you’re doing,” Tuttle said. She added that data consistently shows films made with greater gender balance perform better commercially. “That’s a lot of creative energy that gets wasted,” Tuttle said, referring to the effort women are forced to spend justifying the conversation rather than making work.

	Cameron Bailey, chief executive of the Toronto Film Festival, said the festival’s programming team has maintained around 50% women for more than a decade and that TIFF’s 2026 selection stands at 35% films directed by women, up from 25% a decade ago. He traced the Share Her Journey initiative – launched at TIFF in 2017 by his sister Maxine Bailey – to a conviction that gatekeepers must actively surface work by women. “That kind of stuff is still out there, and it’s quite prevalent, actually,” Bailey said, recalling hearing Academy members ask why they would want to watch Sarah Polley’s “Women Talking” during its Oscar campaign.

	Angèle Diabang, a filmmaker from Senegal, described founding the Mousso Institute in 2022. “Competence is a form of emancipation,” Diabang said. “I don’t want a woman on set because someone wants to tick a box. I want her there because she knows her craft.” Working in cohorts of six in Casamance – her home region, deliberately chosen over the capital Dakar to decentralize opportunity – the institute trains women as cinematographers, sound engineers, lighting technicians and editors, entirely free of charge. Two cohorts, 12 women trained.

	France’s CNC has required all cast, crew and technicians on French productions to undergo gender-based violence training since 2021. From 2027, a bonus-penalty mechanism will link CNC funding to gender targets: productions with fewer than 40% women crew face penalties, while those that meet or exceed the threshold receive a bonus. Canal+ was the first company to join the Safe Place movement, which supports women who are victims of violence both on set and in their daily lives, Marsh noted.
	

	Moderator Patrick Caligiuri, a producer and media advisor, closed by expressing a hope that a future Lumière Summit would not need to hold the panel again.

schema.headline: Film Industry Leaders Demand Structural Fix for Gender Gap at Lumiere Summit

title: Betty Gilpin Jabs at Sam Altman During ‘Manic Poem’ Acceptance Speech at the Emmys
description: “Widow’s Bay” guest star Betty Gilpin accepted her Emmy win for outstanding guest actress in a comedy by reading a poem she had written in jest — an
body:
“Widow’s Bay” guest star Betty Gilpin accepted her Emmy win for outstanding guest actress in a comedy by reading a poem she had written in jest — and very much in the unique style of the show. But it was one line that especially got the TV Academy audience at the Peacock Theatre to cheer: “Let’s all lean toward Sam Shepard and less toward Sam Altman.”

	Gilpin won for playing Sarah Westcott Warren, the long-suffering wife of town founder Richard Warren in the “Widow’s Bay” flashback episode “Our History.”
	

	Here’s her acceptance speech, in poem:


	“If by some fluke you win, a poem might give it a less boring spin. If you lose, whisper it drunk to your date, Allie Brie, whose toned shoulders we stand on for her work in TV. / Thank you, ‘Widows Bay’ residents, [Katie] Dippold, [Hiro] Murai, to Hamish and Apple, our director Ti [West] / To my reps Sean, Jenny, Andrea, Dara and Tony. Is it weird I say love you when we hang up the phony? (Sorry) /

	“Rhymings of vulnerability cloak. What we do means so much to me. That part’s not a joke / Look, my family has nurses, a priest and a teacher. I’m a spray-tanned, narcissistic society leecher. / But I want to thank all of the actors I’ve met — old ladies in dressing rooms, hot guys on sets. What a privilege to spend this life laughing at crafty, watching Shakespeare in theaters, half full and drafty. / 

	“Our business is stupid, but actors are the bomb. From Martindale to Milioti, my dad and my mom, to be cringe and elitist, which you’re free to find fault in. Let’s all lean toward Sam Shepard and less toward Sam Altman. /
	

	“Thank you, Cosmo. My family, my daughters, friends — too many to name — my brothers Sam, Harry and my long dead dog Babe. Thank you.”

	Where did the idea for the poem come from? Gilpin credited her episodic co-star Hamish Linklater, who also earned a guest actor in a comedy Emmy nomination for playing Richard Warren.

	“I was on the same flight over as my co-nominee Hamish Linklater, and he came over to my row and was like, ‘Have you written a speech?’ And I was like, ‘Oh no, no, no! I’m not going to win,’” she said. “He’s like, ‘Well, you need to do that because it’s a scientific possibility, and don’t be stupid. Just prepare something.’ So he scared the shit out of me, and I wrote a quick manic poem, as you know, women have done for centuries. And I love my dog Babe. I named my first daughter after him. I’m almost ready for a dog, decade away.”

	“Widow’s Bay” ended Night 2 of the 78th Emmys with eight wins — the most of any program so far. Gilpin called the recognition “incredible.” 

	“The episode that Hamish and I did, it’s like we did this strange little period indie movie at the end of the actual filming of contemporary ‘Widow’s Bay.’ So it felt like, honestly an island within an island. The crew and writers had filmed all nine episodes before us, and so to encounter all these people who were clearly brilliant and tired and had just taken a big risk, and then to watch that risk pay off immensely — it’s just so satisfying. A point for brilliant, weird, creative people, I’d say.”

	In her episode, Sarah appears to perish as she attempts to leave the island. Is there any chance she might return in another flashback? “I feel like by her genius demented ‘Widow’s Bay’ lore math, it doesn’t make sense for her to come back,” Gilpin said. “But like, come on, just find it so I can come back. I would love to do that. I loved working on the show so much. Katie Dippold’s brain and work and the fact that Apple made her show a reality gives me renewed faith in our industry. Honestly, something so original and niche and strange and human having success in the mainstream — it gives me hope, honestly, that we’re not totally lost in our industry.”

schema.headline: Betty Gilpin Jabs at Sam Altman During ‘Manic Poem’ Acceptance Speech at the Emmys

title: BBC News Anchor Maryam Moshiri Reveals Blood Cancer Diagnosis
description:
BBC News anchor Maryam Moshiri has revealed she has been diagnosed with incurable blood cancer.

	The anchor, who joined the BBC in 2003, has covere
body:
BBC News anchor Maryam Moshiri has revealed she has been diagnosed with incurable blood cancer.

	The anchor, who joined the BBC in 2003, has covered events ranging from the Pope’s funeral to the Iran war since being diagnosed with Polycythaemia vera (PV) two years ago. Moshiri went public with her diagnosis Monday in an interview with The Times of London.

	“I was working 14-hour days, constantly on air, constantly having to think on my feet, and holding it together, despite the fact that I had this chronic tiredness and fatigue,” she told the newspaper. “When you’re doing live news, you have this rush of adrenaline, and you just have to get on with it.”
	

	Although the cancer itself is not deadly, PV results in the overproduction of red blood cells, causing the blood to thicken and potentially leading to blood clots, heart attacks and strokes. It requires lifelong treatment, much of which is physically gruelling.


	“It is going to be there till the day I die,” Moshiri said of her diagnosis. “A big part of this disease is having to get on with life.”

	Among the treatments Moshiri has endured are twice-monthly venesections, where doctors remove blood through a vein, which she said was exhausting and left her feeling “extremely unwell.” Despite that, she travelled to Rome for two weeks last year to cover the death of Pope Francis.

	On her return she underwent an immunotherapy treatment which resulted in “horrendous” side effects. She eventually switched to a different drug.

	Moshri, who also has three children, decided to go public with her diagnosis in order to back a campaign by charity Blood Cancer U.K. called “Here for This,” which highlights the time sufferers miss with loved ones due to their treatment. She is also determined to continue working.
	

	“I love what I do. I love being where the story is,” she told The Times. “I don’t want to allow blood cancer to stop me from doing my work.”

schema.headline: BBC News Anchor Maryam Moshiri Reveals Blood Cancer Diagnosis

title: Ellen Burstyn Cries as She Gets Venice Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement: ‘It’s One Thing to Win an Oscar, Tony or Emmy — All of Which I’ve Won. But This Is a Lot’
description: Maggie Gyllenhaal delivered a message on behalf of Ellen Burstyn before the 93-year-old acting legend took the stage at the Venice Film Festival to
body:
Maggie Gyllenhaal delivered a message on behalf of Ellen Burstyn before the 93-year-old acting legend took the stage at the Venice Film Festival to receive the prestigious Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement.

	“Ellen asked me to let you know that she recently took a fall,” Gyllenhaal said from the podium. “She’s OK, but she is moving more slowly — which is fine because it’ll give us more time to clap.”


	Indeed, the room burst into applause as Burstyn, clad in a vibrant yellow gown, sauntered onto the stage with a walker. Burstyn cried and wiped away her tears with a tissue as she was greeted with a heartfelt, minutes-long standing ovation. 
	

	“You’re making me cry!” she said, which did little to stop the enthusiastic applause. “You’re overwhelming me, you know! I don’t know how to recover from that generous greeting.”

	Burstyn has achieved a lot in her seven-decade career in Hollywood, which she was quick to remind the crowd, but she puts the Venice award among the top honors.

	“You can’t imagine how meaningful this is to me It’s one thing to win an Oscar, a Tony or an Emmy — all of which I’ve won,” she said. “But this … it’s a lot.”

	Since she learned she’d receive the Golden Lion, she said, she’s been reflecting on her life — and what it means to get a career tribute.

	“At 93, it means you have a far about of lifetime to look back on,” she said. “I thought, maybe it’s not just a record of what you’ve accomplished, but what you’ve learned.”

	During her speech, she recalled that while shooting Martin Scorsese’s 1974 drama “Alice Doesn’t Live Here Anymore,” she was required to film a nighttime driving scene while the director and the cinematographer were blocking her view of the street. 
	

	“I couldn’t see the side of the road; I could go off and kill all of us,” Burstyn said. “But then I noticed, this is a two-way road. There’s a white line in the middle of the road, and I can see that. So all I have to do is look up to the left, and follow the white line. And that’s how I managed to not kill Martin Scorsese.” 

	She then drew a parallel between the funny story and the fraught state of the U.S. right now, saying: “I wanted to close out saying how deeply appreciative I am of this Golden Lion and I hope — no, pray — that my own country will find its own white line.”

	Burstyn was awarded the Golden Lion on Monday afternoon during the premiere of Gyllenhaal’s short film “Flesh Impact.” Taika Waititi, Pamela Anderson and Murray Bartlett, her co-stars in “Place to Be,” a comedic drama that premieres Wednesday on the Lido, attended the ceremony. The trio were among the first to lead another standing ovation when Burstyn exited the stage and went to sit in the audience.

	Dedicated to Marilyn Monroe on what would be her 100th birthday, the 20-minute-long “Flesh Impact” portrays Dakota Johnson as the actress at the height of her fame and Burstyn as the version of Monroe the world never got to see. The star died on Aug. 4, 1962 at age 36 from an acute barbiturate overdose. The short’s title, “Flesh Impact,” comes from a phrase once used to describe the aura of Monroe — “that she looked so real and luminous on camera that viewers felt they could touch her through the screen,” according to the synopsis.

	Prior to the ceremony, Burstyn sat on Monday morning for a press conference and spoke about a fleeting encounter with Monroe way back when.

	“We never met. We saw each other once. We went to a nightclub, and she was sitting across from me,” Burstyn recalled. “And of course, I was enchanted by just looking at her. She was such a magical creature. And then she looked at me and nodded at me. And I was very early in my career, and I thought, was I just recognized by Marilyn Monroe?”

	She had another connection to Monroe, through Ralph Roberts, an actor-turned-masseur to the stars.

	“Ralph Roberts, who had been Marilyn’s masseur, and not only that, but her confidant, he had lots of stories to tell me about Marilyn,” Burstyn said. “So I used to get my massages and hear Marilyn’s stories. My favorite one was that her whole persona was a construction.”
	

	Burstyn was asked if she had any other memorable encounters with other Hollywood luminaries, to which she responded, “When I met Marlon Brando briefly, and I almost fainted. That was pretty spectacular.”

	Then, she cracked, “I can’t think of anyone else — it mustn’t have impressed me too much.”She also recalled the early career advice she received from Bette Davis, who was 24 years her senior.

	“I had just become known,” Burstyn said. “I was new, but famous. I met [Davis] and she said, ‘Let me tell you one thing, honey. At the beginning of your illustrious career, the only thing that’s important is your work. Anybody that tries to get in the way of you and your work, they’re your enemy. You know what you say to them? ‘You are my enemy.’ I said, “Thank you, Mrs. Davis…” 

	Burstyn has two movies at Venice, the other being Kornél Mundruczó’s quirky drama “Place to Be,” which premieres on Wednesday. She stars in “Place to Be” alongside Waititi, Anderson, Édgar Ramírez, Lena Waithe and Bartlett. Mundruczó and Burstyn previously collaborated on “Pieces of a Woman,” which premiered on the Lido in 2020. 

	Burstyn, who is still acting as a nonagenarian, described her rationale for saying “yes” to projects.

	“When I get a script, I sit down and read it — and if it makes me laugh, that’s good. If it makes me cry, that’s good. If it makes me laugh and cry, that’s terrific,” she said. “By the time I finish the script, I have to feel moved in some way to say, ‘I want to do this.'”

	As Burstyn mentioned in her Golden Lion Speech, she is one of the few performers to achieve the Triple Crown of Acting, earning an Oscar for “Alice Doesn’t Live Here Anymore” and a Tony for “Same Time, Next Year” in 1975, and two Emmys for “Law & Order: Special Victims Unit” and “Political Animals” in 2009 and 2013, respectively. Over her 60-year career in Hollywood, Burstyn has received dozens of nominations for films and television shows including “The Exorcist,” “The Last Picture Show,” “Requiem for a Dream” and “House of Cards.”

	Burstyn believes roles for women in entertainment have changed “enormously” over the decades. She added that although the industry is “not quite 50-50” in terms of parity, “they’re close.”

	“When I first started working, which was 150 years ago, there were no women on set. No women crew. No women directing. It was all men,” she said. “If a woman was on set, it meant she was an actress. And then slowly, thanks to blessed Gloria Steinem, who just died, the consciousness started to be changed.”

schema.headline: Ellen Burstyn Cries as She Gets Venice Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement: ‘It’s One Thing to Win an Oscar, Tony or Emmy — All of Which I’ve Won. But This Is a Lot’

title: Festival Leaders Confront Growing Political Pressure at Lumiere Summit: ‘We Don’t Judge Artists by Their Passport’
description: Political pressure on film and television festivals emerged as a defining theme of a panel discussion Monday at the Lumière Summit in Saint-Paul-de-
body:
Political pressure on film and television festivals emerged as a defining theme of a panel discussion Monday at the Lumière Summit in Saint-Paul-de-Vence, France, with Séries Mania general director Laurence Herszberg issuing the session’s most direct call for protection of programming autonomy. 

	“We don’t judge artists by their passport, we judge them by their works,” Herszberg said.


	The panel, titled “Easy to Criticize, Impossible to Replace: Rethinking the Festival” and moderated by Rajendra Roy, chief curator of film at MoMA, brought together festival chiefs from Berlin, Cannes, Toronto, San Sebastián, Annecy, Mumbai, Durban, the Red Sea and South by Southwest. It covered three areas: audiences and community, how festivals relate to the media, and the mounting economic and political strains on festival leadership.
	

	Herszberg was direct on the political pressure facing her and her peers. “We feel more and more under pressure from different groups,” she said. “They might be politicians, they might be just people who disagree with the representation of some countries.” As general director of Séries Mania – a free-access festival that featured more than 112.000 participants, 5.200 professionals of the industry and +600 journalists this year – she said controlling who walks through the door is not possible. “We have to be protected, and we still have to go on and fight for the artists,” Herszberg said.


	Cameron Bailey, chief executive of the Toronto Film Festival, which launches its first formal market this year, echoed the sentiment. “Filmmakers are not their nations, and shouldn’t be treated as such by anyone,” Bailey said. He recalled joining TIFF as a programmer in 1990, “at a time when festivals felt like a completely free and open space.” Bailey pointed to TIFF’s Next Wave youth program – now 15 years old – as a long-term investment in building young audiences. “‘Obsession’ became one of the biggest sales at a film festival in a long, long time,” Bailey said, noting that Next Wave participants had championed the title. On the rationale for TIFF’s new market, Bailey said: “The market is also part of that ecosystem – I mean, a terrible way to put it would be that it’s the fertilizer of the ecosystem, but really, it’s what feeds” a constant supply of ambitious films.
	

	Berlinale festival director Tricia Tuttle, whose event drew 450,000 admissions last year, and was at the eye of a political storm, put audience development at the center of her contribution. “The answer for me to all of these challenges is to really think about audiences,” Tuttle said, adding that reaching people who are not yet passionate cinemagoers matters as much as serving those who are.

	Cannes president Iris Knobloch pointed to the breadth of her festival’s annual gathering – 40,000 accredited participants from 140 countries, with over 4,000 journalists in attendance. “For me, that is the real shining light on films and the talent all over the world,” Knobloch said.

	Faisal Baltyuor, chief executive of the Red Sea Film Foundation, said his organization’s last edition sold out every screening. “We have a lot of creative talents that need that boost to make it to the international stage,” Baltyuor said, noting that 11 films the Foundation supported appeared in Venice and eight were heading to Toronto.

	On the festival-press relationship, Peter Debruge – now director of the South by Southwest Film & TV Festival after a 20-year tenure at Variety, the last ten as chief critic – put the case for studio films serving discovery. “The studio-level films are the sizzle that brings the attention, the press, and the audiences to the discoveries,” Debruge said.

	Maialen Beloki, deputy director of San Sebastián, pointed to shrinking press resources as a structural problem. “Each year, media send less and less critics to the festival,” Beloki said. She added that the race to break news online carries its own cost. “We are losing our capacity to talk about the films with some time and with some respect,” Beloki said.

	Shivendra Singh Dungarpur, founding director of the Film Heritage Foundation and director of the MAMI Festival in Mumbai, said his screenings of restored films regularly attract between 1,000 and 1,400 people and that all MAMI events are free of charge. “I believe that a film festival has to be for everyone,” Dungarpur said. He described the MAMI Independent outreach initiative that partnered with a major cinema chain to bring independent films to cities across India ahead of the festival proper.

	Mickaël Marin, from the Annecy Animation Film Festival, said that since his appointment in 2018 he has worked to open Annecy to general audiences beyond its traditional professional base, including through a permanent exhibition space that opened last June. “We have a worldwide community of animation coming here in Annecy, from the school, from the student, up to the platform,” Marin said.
	

	Magdalene Reddy, director of the Durban FilmMart Institute, said the core challenge in Africa is not finding audiences but reaching them in the absence of sufficient cinema infrastructure. “For us, engaging with audiences is really going into the community,” Reddy said. 

	When moderator Roy closed the session by asking whether festivals could survive without the American industry – demanding a yes or no – Reddy was the only panelist to answer no, while noting that her focus remains squarely on African content.

schema.headline: Festival Leaders Confront Growing Political Pressure at Lumiere Summit: ‘We Don’t Judge Artists by Their Passport’

title: ‘Plaza Catedral’ Director Abner Benaim, Chile’s Daniela Vega and Alfredo Castro Board Fiction Series ‘School of the Americas’ (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Panama’s Abner Benaim has boarded as a co-director of the fiction series “School of the Americas” (“Escuela de las Américas”), which will star two o
body:
Panama’s Abner Benaim has boarded as a co-director of the fiction series “School of the Americas” (“Escuela de las Américas”), which will star two of Chile’s most internationally renowned thespians: Daniela Vega, who headed the Oscar-winning “A Fantastic Woman,) and Alfredo Castro, a Pablo Larrain regular who’s also starred in a slew of Latin American projects.

	The project has been selected for the Co-Production and Financing Forum at Madrid-based confab Iberseries & Platino Industria which takes place Sept. 29-Oct. 2.
	

	Benaim was an obvious addition to the project given its subject matter and setting. “School of the Americas” begins with an exhumation at the site of the 1983 El Jazmín massacre, which yields a graduation photograph of four commandos with their faces scratched out and a pendant stamped Fort Gulick, the U.S. military base in the Panama Canal Zone, site of the infamous U.S. Army School of the Americas.


	Panamanian-American human rights investigator Inés Vega recognizes the massacre’s signature: counterinsurgency doctrine taught at the School. When someone tries to kill her, the cold case turns personal. Tracking four graduates across three continents, she uncovers what the School really taught – and who is still protecting its legacy.

	Benaim joins co-director Oscar Godoy who also has close ties to Larraín, having been first AD on Larraín’s “The Count,” “The Club,” “Neruda,” “No” and “Tony Manero.” Godoy was recently second unit director on Fabula’s “Someone Has to Know,” which ranked among Netflix’s global top ten for non-English-language series.
	

	His feature “Ulysses” screened at a string of festivals, starting with the San Sebastián Film Fest and culminating at Chile’s Santiago Film Fest (Sanfic) where it won Best Chilean Film.

	Benaim, Panama’s most internationally renowned filmmaker, has represented his country three times at the Oscars, starting with his documentary “Invasion,” about the U.S. 1989 invasion of Panama, followed by “Yo No Me Llamo Rubén Blades” and “Plaza Catedral,” the latter making the Academy shortlist and earning Benaim a Premios Platino nomination for screenplay. His debut feature “Chance” remains the highest-grossing Panamanian film ever released.

	Its producers Seedling Media Productions (Panama) and La Panda Productions (U.S./Spain) are targeting 2028 for principal photography to begin, provided all the financing is in place.

	“The School of the Americas was a real school, located in the Panama Canal Zone; for half a century, it taught officers from across Latin America. We are not making a series about monsters — monsters are an alibi. We are making one about a curriculum: the fact that this was written down, graded and taught, and the men who graduated went home and became somebody’s father. Violence isn’t born. It’s taught,” said La Panda’s Guillermo Escalona, co-creator and executive producer alongside Brittany DeVries of Seedling Media.

	Escalona, a Spanish-American screenwriter-producer based in Los Angeles, co-founder of La Panda Productions, is the co-creator and co-writer, along with Rhayuela’s Federico Durán, of the late Colombian filmmaker Jaime Osorio Márquez’s posthumous feature “The Awakening.” The supernatural action thriller was completed by Durán and José Luis Rugeles (“Alias Maria” “Rebellion”) after the director’s death following which it world-premiered at the Guadalajara International Film Festival in April, with Latido Films handling sales.

	Based in Panama, Seedling Media Productions, founded in 2013 by DeVries, has a varied list of credits that include fiction and documentary features. Among them are crime thriller “Chacalería,” “I Really Love My Husband,” shot in Panama and premiered at SXSW in 2025 and documentaries “Dear Panamá,” “A World Without Orphans” and “Lost Kites,” winner of the Best Documentary Feature at the London Independent Film Awards.
	

	Currently, Seedling is producing “Against No One” (“Denuncia Contra Nadie”), a co-production with Guatemala supported by the Ibermedia Co-Production Fund.

schema.headline: ‘Plaza Catedral’ Director Abner Benaim, Chile’s Daniela Vega and Alfredo Castro Board Fiction Series ‘School of the Americas’ (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Studio TF1 Smashes Doc Records With ‘Leon Marchand: Beyond Gold,’ Rolls Out ‘Surface’
description: Studio TF1 is celebrating recent successes at home and abroad with Sacha Vucinic and Xavier Marchand’s sports documentary “Leon Marchand: Beyond Gol
body:
Studio TF1 is celebrating recent successes at home and abroad with Sacha Vucinic and Xavier Marchand’s sports documentary “Leon Marchand: Beyond Gold” and Slimane-Baptiste Berhoun’s mystery drama “Surface.”

	While the doc series on French Olympic swimming champion Leon Marchand and his life in the wake of four gold-medal wins at the Paris Olympics has scored record viewing results for France TV, “Surface” has proved a hot seller across Europe and in the U.S.
	

	Offering an intimate look at the young Marchand over the year following his Olympic victories, “Leon Marchand: Beyond Gold” goes beyond the medals to explore his identity, ambition and life as he copes with sudden fame, pursues engineering studies and navigates personal growth at age 22.


	Setting an all-time documentary record for France TV, the three-part series drew 2.3 million average views per episode when it premiered on the france.tv platform in July followed by 1.6 million viewers on France 2 during its Sept. 1 TV premiere and a total of more than 13 million views across social media, including more than 1 million views on YouTube.   



	

					‘Surface’
									Baptiste Langinier/France Télévisions/Quad Drama
	



	On the scripted front, Studio TF1’s hit mystery drama “Surface,” which premiered last year at Canneseries and went on to become a major hit on France TV’s streaming platform, has found enthusiastic buyers abroad.

	Based on the bestselling novel by Olivier Norek and produced by Quad Drama for France TV, the show has sold to MHz Choice in the U.S., the BBC in the U.K., AMC Global Media in Spain, Vodafone for Greece, Blue Play for French-speaking Switzerland and to Moment in a deal covering airlines and cruise ships.
	

	Also presented last year at the Unifrance Rendez-Vous in Le Havre, the six-part series follows Parisian police captain Noémie Chastain, who is visiting a remote town to assess a police station’s possible closure while recovering from a traumatic facial injury.

	When the discovery of a child’s remains leads to the reopening a 20-year-old missing person’s case, Chastain decides to lead the investigation herself, in the process uncovering dark secrets that impact both her and the town.

schema.headline: Studio TF1 Smashes Doc Records With ‘Leon Marchand: Beyond Gold,’ Rolls Out ‘Surface’

title: ‘Imperium’ Review: Sergei Loznitsa Brings Together Nearly Three Hours of Italian Footage From the Early 1970s Covering the Vastness of the USSR
description: In the early 1970s, Italian film crews spread out across the USSR, capturing a vast, multicultural empire few had ever seen in such diversity. From
body:
In the early 1970s, Italian film crews spread out across the USSR, capturing a vast, multicultural empire few had ever seen in such diversity. From urban commuters to village fêtes, Baku trawlers to Siberian reindeer herders, the cameramen aimed to capture the Soviet polity at a time when Westerners had a gray, monolithic image of what lay behind the Iron Curtain. Granted official permission, they managed to resist any push towards propaganda, even finding ways to slyly critique a system that proclaimed regional autonomy but controlled everything from the Kremlin. While planned as a monumental, multi-chapter TV series, only a few episodes wound up being broadcast on Italian TV, just once, following which the endeavor lay forgotten in the archives. If ever there was a project for Sergei Loznitsa, this was it.
	

	In “Imperium,” working with 60 hours of 16mm, the master documentarian organizes this journey along geographic lines, starting in Moscow and heading east, then doubling back through “the Stans” and the Baltic republics until ending in what was then Leningrad. As with Loznitsa’s past films of this type, some snippets of conversation and music have been added, but otherwise the footage has simply been restored and edited together. What’s revealed is an immense state whose distinct regions still managed to hold onto unique traditions, notwithstanding an incessant centralized proclamation of unity.


	While “Imperium” can be engrossing, its nearly three-hour running time is felt more than in Loznitsa masterpieces like “Maidan” and “State Funeral.” Perhaps that’s because in those films, one feels the force of history pushing us forward, inexorably heading to a watershed moment whose impact continues to resonate across the decades. With “Imperium,” the motivation is clear yet the concept is more diffuse. It’s also a film which will likely resonate best with those of us old enough to recall how the Soviet Union was discussed in the West at the time, a decade before Ronald Reagan’s “Evil Empire” remark — which simply gave a reductivist Star Wars moniker to the anti-communist propaganda suffusing American-driven global discourse since the end of the Second World War. For Loznitsa, of course, his interest is inside the country rather than how it was perceived from abroad, though it will be impossible for most audiences to separate the two.
	

	The film kicks off with a classic parade in Red Square for the 24th Congress of the Central Committee of the Communist Party, with banners touting the same slogans from the previous forty years about production targets being met ahead of schedule. Next comes the GUM department store and window displays with tuxedos, shiny patent leather shoes and beaded handbags, making us wonder who in early 1970s Moscow was buying such luxury goods. Commercialized religion makes its first appearance with a lively trade in Christmas decorations, one of many reminders that despite an official policy of atheism, certain traditions were allowed to persist. (Vladimir Putin, of course, has done an even better job in harnessing religion to his oligarchic dictatorship.)

	From the capital the footage moves east, where consumer goods are far more difficult to obtain. In Suzdal, an old woman washes clothes in an ice hole; shots of Vladimir show a town seemingly unchanged from pre-Revolutionary days; further south, residents come out for a winter carnival whose roots must date long before Leninism arrived. As the cameramen spread east, local customs become stronger: Bactrian camel races near the Mongolian border, reindeer sleds in the Sakha Republic. It’s here in Siberia where the footage most forcefully critiques Soviet policy, as a group of young Caucasian Russians (in classic 1970s fashion) play guitar and sing Russian songs, the local Yakut population looking on from the sidelines, discontented observers of this not-so-subtle form of colonialism.

	The greatest takeaway from “Imperium” is just how stubbornly resistant centuries-old traditions were to the Soviet push towards uniformity. People still attended mosques in Bukhara and churches in Etchmiadzin, they held on to ways of life that had not been collectivized by Stalinist dictates. Today, however, rampant capitalism and the internet have changed Russia’s social landscape far more than anything Lenin or Brezhnev could have imagined, turning stubbornly multicultural populations that boldly resisted homogeneity into consumers looking West for their acquisitions.

	It’s interesting to imagine what might have happened had Italian TV screened the majority of these films upon release. A sense of what life was really like in the Soviet Union was hard to come by then — in the U.S., a 1977 National Geographic publication “Journey Across Russia: The Soviet Union Today” was the first populist corrective to the sense of a uniform society of collectivized proletariat. 
	

	Italy, with its strong communist party, had a different problem, too often refusing to acknowledge Politburo abuses. An interesting companion piece to “Imperium” would be Federico Ferrone and Michele Manzolini’s 2013 documentary “The Train to Moscow: A Journey to Utopia,” also consisting of found footage but earlier, when a party supporter from Emilia Romagna discovered that life in the USSR wasn’t all solidarity and freedom. At the time, his Italian colleagues censored his revelations. All empires peddle utopias, but why do so many people believe them?

schema.headline: ‘Imperium’ Review: Sergei Loznitsa Brings Together Nearly Three Hours of Italian Footage From the Early 1970s Covering the Vastness of the USSR

title: ‘Sumo: Spirit Weighs Nothing’ Review: A Handsome Ode to an Oft-Disrespected Sport
description: The title of “Sumo: Spirit Weighs Nothing” is the closest that Erik Shirai‘s documentary comes to a joke at the expense of its subject: sumo wrestli
body:
The title of “Sumo: Spirit Weighs Nothing” is the closest that Erik Shirai‘s documentary comes to a joke at the expense of its subject: sumo wrestling, the Japanese sport largely known in the western world for the ample size and minimal clothing of its practitioners, and not an awful lot beyond that. In all other respects, however, this stately, artfully produced film aims to act as a corrective to such cheap, culturally insensitive perceptions. Examining as it does the motivations and ambitions of a number of sumo wrestlers, from grand masters to rising stars, through a solemnly respectful lens, the doc finds humanity and even beauty in what can all too easily be comically framed on screen.
	

	Indeed, the approach of Japanese-American docmaker Shirai (who previously probed a very different Japanese institution in his popular 2015 doc “The Birth of Saké”) is so respectful as to feel a touch sanitized: smoothed-out and simplified for the benefit of Western viewers, to whose perspective the film is mostly tailored. More unsavory aspects of the sport — including controversies over hazing and match-fixing, not to mention its ongoing exclusion of women from competition and ceremonies — are swept aside, while the compelling fact of its declining popularity in Japan is only passingly addressed. Only before the closing credits roll is it revealed how few yokozuna (the name given to men achieving the highest rank in sumo) this century have been homegrown, as Mongolia and the U.S. step into the breach.


	Shedding more light on such matters would provide a richer context for the film’s reverent celebration of sumo tradition, but many viewers will still find it an illuminating and exquisitely mounted study, ennobling the sport with the sheer, studied splendor of its imagery, captured alternately in atmospherically high-contrast monochrome and tea-stained sepia tones. Produced by ESPN Films, it will doubtless find a dedicated broadcast and streaming viewership following its premiere as the opening film of Venice’s audience-oriented Spotlight competition.
	

	Early on, the camera observes a group of rookie wrestlers, training at the Tokyo stable of 62-year-old Master Sakaigawa, as they collectively recite a pledge to the sport: “We shall uphold our responsibility and duty to to sumo; we shall uphold a strong heart, kindness and courage.” This is followed by a droll shot of trainees all putting their freshly laundered thongs out to dry: For all its earnestness, the film is not without offhand humor. In the house of Sakaigawa, we meet Hiradoumi, a 24-year-old upstart tipped for big things in the ring (or dohyō, to use its proper term), and a great hope for continued Japanese representation in the sport’s top tier. In the same stable, and younger still, is teenager Yonezawaryu, still learning the ropes, and battling doubts over his long-term commitment to sumo after witnessing firsthand the extreme, potentially fatal, physical toll it takes on the body.

	At the opposite end of the career scale is Mongolian-born Terunofuji, who at the time of filming was the only practicing yokozuna in sumo, a 10-time title winner considering retirement after 14 years in the sport, five of them at the very top. He is spoken of as a veteran, positively godly in status, though he’s only 33 years old. Age, however, doesn’t mean quite what it does to civilians in a realm where so much transformational strain is placed on the body, and Terunofuji’s is beginning to fail him. “By doing sumo, I’m cutting my lifespan by 10 to 20 years,” he frankly admits, before likening the travails of the professional wrestler to those of a soldier going to war. He’s now married with a son — it’s hard not to wonder if, at the end of his reign, he thinks it was all worth it.

	It’s one of a few questions that this handsome, sober documentary is too polite to ask. But it does convey the grand, challenging physicality of sumo, which to many of its students qualifies as an answer in itself. There’s also a thoughtful focus here on the pain and labor that goes into building and maintaining these extraordinary bodies — shot, by Shirai and fellow DP Hiroshi Hara, in awed chiaroscuro portraits that line up with the men’s view of themselves as warriors of a kind, leaving far behind many racist, cartoonish depictions of yore.

schema.headline: ‘Sumo: Spirit Weighs Nothing’ Review: A Handsome Ode to an Oft-Disrespected Sport

title: Egyptian TV Host Sentenced to Death by Hanging in Drug Trafficking Case
description:
Egyptian TV Host
                          Sentenced to Death by Hanging for Drug Trafficking
body:
Egyptian TV Host
                          Sentenced to Death by Hanging for Drug Trafficking
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 6, 2026
                            5:45 PM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  September 7, 2026
                                5:18 AM PDT
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            An Egyptian TV host broke down in tears in court after learning her fate in a massive drug trafficking case ... death by hanging.
      
    
            Sarah Khalifa, a 39-year-old former host of the Egyptian crime show "Mission Impossible," was sentenced to death in Cairo after being convicted of helping run an organized drug operation.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            She and 11 others were sentenced to death after prosecutors accused the group of importing raw materials used to manufacture synthetic drugs and storing the finished product inside residential homes.
      

            Khalifa reportedly sobbed as the sentence was handed down, pleading with the court and insisting she didn't need money from drugs. She denies the allegations, reportedly telling investigators she'd never even smoked a cigarette.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Authorities say the sprawling case involved 28 defendants and led to the seizure of more than 1,600 pounds of narcotics, along with unlicensed guns and ammunition.
      
    
            Nine other defendants were sentenced to life in prison, while seven were acquitted.
      
    
            Khalifa -- who also ran a cosmetic surgery clinic and an event-planning company -- was arrested in 2025.
      
    
            The death sentence was issued after the court consulted Egypt's grand mufti, a required step in Egyptian capital cases ... and the ruling can still be appealed.

title: Burning Man Attendee Found Dead at Campsite, Second Death at Festival
description:
Burning Man
                          Attendee Found Dead in Campsite
                          D
body:
Burning Man
                          Attendee Found Dead in Campsite
                          Days After First Death
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 7, 2026
                            9:10 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            A second Burning Man attendee has died during this year’s festival ... and this time, the participant was found dead inside his own campsite.
      
    
            According to the Burning Man Project, 60-year-old Craigh Mann was discovered by fellow campers Saturday afternoon at the Nevada event. No cause of death has been released at this time.
      
    
            The tragedy comes just days after another man in his 50s died following a medical emergency at the festival. As TMZ previously reported, he was treated with lifesaving measures before being taken to the event’s emergency care center, where he was pronounced dead.
      
    
            Authorities said there were no immediate signs of foul play in that incident. While the man’s identity remained private pending family notification, the Burning Man Project confirmed Mann’s death.
      
    
            The two deaths come one year after 37-year-old Vadim Kruglov was found fatally stabbed inside a tent during Burning Man. As we previously reported at the time, Kruglov had been missing for several days before authorities identified him as the festival’s first homicide victim.
      
    
            The investigation into Kruglov’s killing remains open, with no suspect publicly identified. The cause of Mann’s death will be determined by the medical examiner.

title: Macklemore Faces Calls to Be Dropped From Ed Sheeran Tour Over Pro-Palestine Set
description:
Macklemore
                          Facing Calls to Boot Him From Ed Sheeran Tour
body:
Macklemore
                          Facing Calls to Boot Him From Ed Sheeran Tour
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 6, 2026
                            5:15 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Macklemore is catching serious heat for turning his opening set on Ed Sheeran's tour into a political statement ... and now an Israeli-American group wants him booted from the remaining shows.
      
    
            The "Thrift Shop" rapper opened for Ed Friday and Saturday at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey, where he used part of his set to voice support for Palestinians and rip Israel's conduct in Gaza.
      
    
        Waiting for your permission to load the Twitter Tweet.
      
    
            Macklemore repeatedly shouted "Free Palestine" and performed his 2024 protest track "Hind's Hall" as images tied to Gaza and pro-Palestinian demonstrations flashed behind him.
      

            That didn't sit well with the Israeli-American Council, which has launched a petition calling on Sheeran and tour organizers to dump Macklemore from the rest of the "Loop" tour ... arguing fans paid for a concert, not a political rally.
      
    
            The petition does not publicly show how many signatures it has collected.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The reaction online has been predictably fiery ... with some concertgoers saying they walked out and accusing Macklemore of pushing antisemitic rhetoric, while others defended his decision to use the stage to speak about the war.
      
    
            As TMZ has previously reported ... Macklemore has been outspoken on the Israel-Palestine conflict for years.
      
    
            Back in 2024, singer-songwriter Matisyahu ripped "Hind's Hall" as antisemitic ... telling TMZ he believed the song was only making an already ugly divide worse.
      
    
            Macklemore also sparked outrage that same year when he chanted "f*** America" during a pro-Palestinian festival in Seattle.

title: Rob Reiner Wins Posthumous Emmy for ‘The Bear’ Months After Death
description:
Rob Reiner
                          Wins Emmy for Role in ‘The Bear’
                          M
body:
Rob Reiner
                          Wins Emmy for Role in ‘The Bear’
                          Months After Tragic Death
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 7, 2026
                            5:26 AM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  September 7, 2026
                                6:08 AM PDT
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Rob Reiner is still getting honored by Hollywood ... winning a posthumous Emmy for his role in “The Bear” months after he and his wife were found dead.
      
    
            The late actor took home Outstanding Guest Actor in a Comedy Series at the 2026 Creative Arts Emmys Sunday night for playing Albert Schnurr, a businessman who helps Ebraheim develop a plan to expand The Beef's sandwich window.
      
    
      
      Standing O for the late Rob Reiner, who won Guest Actor in A Comedy Series for The Bear #emmys pic.twitter.com/MX2t1mL7xN
              @gerradhall
          
  
    
            Wendi McLendon-Covey accepted the award on Rob's behalf ... and the room erupted in a standing ovation. She told the crowd, “We all wish he was here.”
      
    
            The Emmy marks Rob’s third win, and his first in nearly 50 years. He previously won for playing Michael “Meathead” Stivic on “All in the Family” in 1974 and 1978.
      
    
            As we’ve previously reported, Rob and his wife, Michele Singer Reiner, were found dead in their Los Angeles home in December. Their son, Nick Reiner, has been charged with two counts of first-degree murder and has pleaded not guilty.
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            “The Bear” also paid tribute to Rob during its series finale ... with Ebraheim calling Albert to share news about franchising The Beef before signing off with “as you wish,” a nod to Rob’s classic film “The Princess Bride.”
      
    
            Rob is expected to receive another tribute during the televised Emmys’ In Memoriam segment later this month.

title: Firefighters Try to Rescue People From Cockpit After Deadly Amazon Plane Crash, Video Shows
description:
Amazon Cargo Plane Crash
                          Firefighters Try To Save Survivors From Cockpit
body:
Amazon Cargo Plane Crash
                          Firefighters Try To Save Survivors From Cockpit
                          New Video Shows
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 7, 2026
                            5:18 AM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  September 7, 2026
                                6:08 AM PDT
                                    
              
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Firefighters sprang into action, trying to pull survivors from a charred cockpit after Sunday's deadly Amazon cargo plane disaster in Miami ... and new video shows the dramatic rescue attempt.
      
    
      
      Emergency crews doused an Amazon Prime Air cargo plane that overran the runway while landing at Miami International Airport on Sunday, killing at least five people and injuring five others.The crash prompted a roughly 3-hour ground stop at the airport as emergency crews… pic.twitter.com/I9ivZ7oAOJ
              @CBSNews
  
    
            In the video ... you can see several firefighters standing around a ladder extending from the tarmac to the plane's cockpit window.
      
    
            Another firefighter is perched on the top of the ladder, trying to remove people from inside the plane through the open window.
      

            Firefighters are also seen hosing down one of the wings at the rear of the Amazon cargo plane, which flew from San Juan, Puerto Rico, to Miami International Airport.
      
    
      
      Footage reveals the crash of 21 Air Flight 7598, which overran the runway at Miami International Airport, resulting in at least 5 fatalities and an unspecified number of injuries. pic.twitter.com/GlYa76KOvA
              @NewsNowUS
          
  
    
            As we reported ... 5 people were killed, and 5 others were injured when the plane overshot the airport's runway and crashed into vehicles on a highway nearby before coming to a halt in a field. Some of the people were trapped inside their vehicles.
      
    
            The Miami-Dade County Fire Rescue said 3 of the injured victims were listed in critical condition at a hospital ... and the 2 others were also hospitalized after being assessed, but their conditions were not released.
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            Dispatch audio from Broadcastify revealed that the plane collided with a truck on the roadway. Authorities said one of the 5 people killed was found under the plane's right wing.
      
    
            Firefighters rushed to the scene to put out flames that had erupted in the smoking carcass of the aircraft. Fox News reported that a fire flared inside one of the engines.
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            The Federal Aviation Administration and the National Transportation Safety Board are investigating. Flights were grounded for most of the afternoon at Miami International Airport after the incident.

schema.headline: Firefighters Try to Rescue People From Cockpit After Deadly Amazon Plane Crash, Video Shows
